title: Cookie Practices in Social Impact Platforms and DoGood Cookie Policy

categories.title: Common Types of Cookies on Social Impact Platforms
categories.description: Global social impact and charity platforms typically use cookies grouped into several categories for different purposes. The main types include:

examples.description: These are essential for basic site functionality and security. They enable core features like user logins, account authentication, and secure checkout, and without them the website cannot operate properly. For example, a session cookie might keep you logged in as you navigate pages, or a security cookie might verify your actions (e.g. a CSRF token or a spam protection token). Because these cookies are necessary to deliver the service, users cannot opt-out of them (other than by disabling cookies in their browser entirely).

These cookies enhance the user experience by remembering preferences and supporting additional features. They are not strictly required, but they help “remember” choices you’ve made to personalize your experience. For instance, functional cookies may remember your chosen language, keep you logged in on return visits, or retain form data so you don’t have to re-enter information. Some platforms integrate tools like HubSpot for customer service or chat features; HubSpot’s cookies, for example, can store information you enter in forms or chats and recognize you when you return, saving you from retyping details. Functional cookies may also support social sharing widgets or embedding content (like a YouTube video), enabling those features on the site.

These cookies collect data about how visitors use the website, helping organizations measure traffic and improve site performance[5]. Analytics cookies allow platforms to understand which pages are popular, how long users stay, and how they interact with the site, so that the site can be optimized and content improved. Crucially, reputable analytics tools are set up to avoid identifying users personally. For example, Google Analytics is widely used to gather aggregate usage statistics; it typically logs information like page views and IP address, but not your name or personal details, and it does not combine analytics data with any personally identifying information[6]. Other analytics and user experience tools like Hotjar or Microsoft Clarity are also common – these can record anonymized session information (e.g. mouse clicks, scrolling, or screen recordings) to help improve the site’s design and fix issues[7]. Analytics cookies are only set if the user has consented to them (especially in EU regions) because they are not strictly necessary.

Many platforms, even in the social impact space, use advertising or targeting cookies to promote their mission and reach audiences via ads. These cookies track your browsing habits and engagement with the site’s content and ads, so the platform (or its partners) can show you relevant promotions or measure the effectiveness of marketing campaigns. For example, a Meta Pixel (Facebook cookie) might record when you click on a DoGood ad on Facebook and later sign up on the DoGood site, allowing the platform to measure ad conversions and tailor future ads to interested users. Similarly, Google Ads cookies can track ad performance and enable personalized advertising on Google’s networks – if you opt in, Google’s cookies help serve you more relevant ads based on your site usage and other data Google holds. These targeting cookies may also limit the number of times you see an ad and help build audiences for outreach. Because advertising cookies can profile users, consent is required in jurisdictions like the EU before setting them, and users must have an opportunity to opt out in places like California.

categories.moreInfo: In addition to the above, some platforms might define categories slightly differently (for instance, some treat “Functional” and “Necessary” as one group of Essential Cookies, while others separate “Performance” vs “Analytics”). But in general, these four categories – Necessary, Functional, Analytics, and Advertising – are standard in cookie policies for modern websites, including volunteer and social good platforms

categories.title: Common Cookie Tools and Integrations in Global Platforms
categories.description: Platforms similar to DoGood typically rely on a range of third-party tools that set cookies to provide analytics, marketing, and enhanced functionality. Key integrations often include:

examples.description: Nearly all major sites use Google Analytics for traffic analytics. It places cookies (like _ga) to count unique visitors and understand user behavior on the site. Google Analytics data helps site owners see aggregate metrics such as how often pages are visited, without identifying individuals. Notably, Google Analytics only uses device identifiers (like IP address on the date of visit) and does not collect personal names or contact info, and many platforms explicitly state they don’t combine Google Analytics data with any personally identifiable information. Data from Google Analytics may be processed on Google’s servers in the United States, so some user information (e.g. IP and cookie ID) can be transmitted internationally for analysis.

If the platform runs advertising campaigns via Google, it will use Google’s advertising cookies (gcl, IDE, etc.) to measure ad effectiveness and enable re-marketing. For example, Google Ads cookies allow a site like DoGood to see which Google ads led to user sign-ups or donations. With consent, these cookies also enable personalized ads* – meaning Google can show you DoGood ads that are more relevant based on your past interactions. (Opting out of these cookies doesn’t mean you stop seeing ads, but the ads may be less tailored to your interests.)

Social impact platforms commonly use the Meta (Facebook) Pixel for advertising and social media analytics. This integration sets cookies that track when a user interacts with a Facebook/Instagram ad and then takes an action on the website (such as signing up or making a donation). The Meta Pixel helps platforms measure ROI on ads and build audiences (for example, creating a “lookalike” audience of people similar to their site’s donors). Data collected via these cookies is sent to Meta’s servers (often in the U.S.) and is subject to Meta’s data policies. Users can typically opt out of personalized ads through their Facebook account ad preferences.

examples.type: Hotjar and Similar User Experience Analytics
examples.description: To improve website design and usability, many platforms use tools like Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity, or FullStory. These services set cookies (_hj* cookies in Hotjar’s case) to track a visitor’s session and link pages viewed into a continuous record. They might record anonymized user interactions – e.g. heatmaps of where users click, how far they scroll, or even screen recordings – which help the site owners identify confusing elements or technical issues. For instance, Microsoft’s Clarity analytics (an equivalent behavior tool) logs page views, time on page, clicks, and even provides playback of sessions. Importantly, such tools typically mask or exclude any personal data (like form entries) from recordings for privacy. Cookies from these tools are categorized as analytics/performance cookies and are only activated with user consent in regions that require it.

HubSpot is a Customer Relationship Management (CRM) and marketing platform widely used by nonprofits and social enterprises to manage contacts and communications. If integrated, HubSpot sets several cookies (like `hubspotutk) to track user interactions on the site and to remember them over multiple visits. DoGood might use HubSpot for things like newsletter sign-ups, volunteer inquiries, or live chat support. HubSpot’s cookies can store information a user provides in web forms or chat so that if you return later, the site “recognizes” you and can load your info or route you to the same representative. HubSpot cookies also help track what pages a user visits and how they engage with DoGood’s content, which assists in tailoring follow-up communications or identifying interested users (for example, flagging that a user looked at volunteering opportunities in education). Because HubSpot involves personal data storage (like your name/email when you fill a form), its cookies are typically categorized as functional/analytics. They will not be set unless you consent, and HubSpot provides its own cookie controls that can be integrated into a consent banner.

Segment is a customer data platform that some tech-forward social good apps use to streamline data from various sources. If DoGood uses Segment’s analytics.js on the site, Segment will set cookies (e.g. ajs_anonymous_id) to assign you a unique identifier and track events (page views, sign-ups, etc.). Segment acts as a pipe that sends these events to other services (like Google Analytics, email marketing tools, etc.), so its cookie helps unify your activity across those tools. Essentially, Segment cookies ensure that once you consent, your analytics and marketing data is consistently collected and correlated. Segment’s cookies do not directly identify you by name; they use an anonymous ID unless you log in or provide info, at which point the cookie can tie to your user account for analytics purposes. As with other analytics cookies, Segment’s cookies would only load after appropriate consent, and Segment can be configured to respect Do Not Track or consent signals.

Depending on features, DoGood might use additional third-party services that set cookies. For example, if the platform shows embedded videos (YouTube/Vimeo), those services set cookies to remember your video preferences and track views. If social media share buttons are present, networks like Twitter or LinkedIn may set cookies (often categorized as Social Media or Targeting cookies). Also, cloud infrastructure or security services (like Cloudflare) might place a cookie for load balancing or bot detection. Each of these would fall into one of the categories above (e.g. a Cloudflare cookie is usually strictly necessary for security).

categories.moreInfo: In summary, **common tools integrated into social impact platforms include Google Analytics, Google Ads, Meta/Facebook Pixel, Hotjar (or similar UX analytics), HubSpot, and Segment**, among others. All these tools set cookies or similar tracking technologies. A comprehensive cookie policy needs to list these and explain their purpose, which is what we will do for DoGood below.

categories.title: Consent Management: GDPR vs CCPA Approaches
categories.description: **User consent** for cookies is handled somewhat differently under the EU’s GDPR and California’s CCPA, and leading platforms adapt their cookie banners accordingly to comply with both:

examples.description: Under GDPR (and the related ePrivacy Directive), prior explicit consent is required before setting any non-essential cookies on a user’s device. This means when an EU user visits the site, they should see a cookie banner or pop-up that does not drop analytics or advertising cookies until the user actively opts in. The consent must be a clear affirmative action – e.g. clicking “Accept All” or selecting specific cookie preferences – and cannot be implied by silence or just continuing to browse. In practice, global platforms show a cookie consent notice on first visit stating that the site uses cookies and offering the user options: for example, buttons like “Accept All Cookies” and “Manage Preferences.” Many also include a “Reject All” option to allow refusal as easily as acceptance (which some EU regulators recommend). Only Strictly Necessary cookies load by default, while categories like Analytics, Functional, and Advertising are only activated if the user consents to each category. Platforms often use a Consent Management Platform (CMP) tool (such as OneTrust, CookieYes, or Cookiebot) to implement this banner and store the user’s choices. For instance, Target Aid (a social impact platform) notes that “where required by law, when you first visit the Website, you will be asked to consent to the use of cookies… and if you accept we will use these technologies.”. This reflects the GDPR approach of obtaining opt-in consent on the first visit. Users can also revoke or change their consent later via a settings link, per GDPR’s requirement that consent be as easy to withdraw as to give.

The California Consumer Privacy Act has a different approach. Prior consent for cookies is generally not required (except for certain sensitive data or minors), but users must be given the right to opt out of the “sale” of their personal information. In the context of cookies, “selling” personal info can include sharing data with third-party ad networks via tracking cookies. So, while a California user might not see as aggressive a cookie banner as in the EU, the site is obligated to inform them of data collection and provide a “Do Not Sell My Personal Information” link or equivalent mechanism to opt out of third-party data sharing. Many US-based platforms simply display a short notice (“We use cookies to improve your experience...”) with an “Accept” button for acknowledgment, and include a link (often in the footer or within the banner) for “Do Not Sell My Info” or “Cookie Settings” to handle opt-outs. The CCPA essentially functions on an opt-out model: by default, cookies can be set, but the user can later refuse the sale/sharing of data. With the 2023 CPRA amendments, sharing for targeted advertising is explicitly covered, and users can opt out of not just “sale” but also “sharing” for cross-context behavioral advertising. Leading platforms therefore ensure that if a user clicks “Do Not Sell” or turns off marketing cookies in a preference center, the site will disable any cookies that would share data with third parties for advertising.

Because DoGood will likely have a global audience, it’s common to use a geo-sensitive banner or a unified approach that satisfies both laws. For example, a platform might always display a full GDPR-style consent banner to all users worldwide – this approach, while strict, ensures compliance everywhere (many companies choose to err on the side of more privacy protection globally). Alternatively, some implement a banner that changes based on region: EU visitors see an opt-in choice, while US visitors see a notice with opt-out information. In either case, an effective practice is to include a “Privacy Preference Center” or cookie settings dialog on the site. This allows users at any time to review and change their cookie preferences by category (e.g. toggling Analytics or Advertising cookies on/off). Many sites store the user’s consent choice in a strictly necessary cookie (often named something like cookieConsent=yes), so that once a user has made their selection, the site remembers it on subsequent visits. Users can then revisit the preferences via a link (for example, “Cookie Settings” in the footer) if they change their mind.

categories.moreInfo: In summary, **GDPR requires an opt-in cookie banner with granular controls, whereas CCPA requires transparency and an easy opt-out** (notably via a “Do Not Sell” link). DoGood will comply with both by presenting a robust consent mechanism: no non-essential cookies for EU users until consent is given, and a clear option for California and other users to opt out of targeted cookie use.

categories.title: Cookie Banners and Opt-in Flows in Practice
categories.description:
**Leading platforms’ cookie banners** usually have a similar look and feel, adhering to these principles. Typically, when you land on a site like GlobalGiving or VolunteerMatch, a pop-up will inform you that the site uses cookies and ask you to make a choice. For example, GlobalGiving’s banner presents buttons for “Accept All”, “Reject All (except required)”, and “Cookies Settings”, along with a brief message about cookie use and a link to the full Cookie Policy (often titled “Privacy Preference Center”). This lets users quickly either accept everything or reject non-essential cookies, or click through to pick and choose categories.

In the preference center (the detailed settings panel), cookies are usually listed by category with toggles: - **Strictly Necessary** is typically ON and disabled (you can’t turn these off because the site wouldn’t work). The description might say these cookies are always active for core functionality. - **Functional, Analytics, Advertising** categories have toggles that default to OFF until you opt-in (for GDPR regions). Users can read descriptions of each category (often similar to what we described above) and enable one, all, or none according to their comfort.

The banner and settings are designed in a **plain-language** way – e.g. “These cookies help us analyze site usage to improve your experience” for Analytics, or “These cookies enable personalized ads” for Advertising – so that non-technical users can understand what they are agreeing to. Good practice (and some regulations) dictate that rejecting cookies should be as easy as accepting. So the banner will either have a visible “Reject” button or at least make the “Settings” easy to find so a user can decline cookies without undue effort.

examples.description: Once a choice is made, the site will typically drop a small necessary cookie recording the consent decision (yes or no per category). This prevents the banner from reappearing on every page load and serves as proof of consent. Users can revisit the preferences anytime (commonly via a “Cookie Settings” link in the website footer or in their account settings). If a user deletes their cookies or visits from a new device/browser, the banner will appear again to obtain consent afresh.

When Big Life Foundation implemented their cookie consent, they explicitly noted that if a user doesn’t consent to optional cookies, those cookies remain inactive. - Projects Abroad’s site states it uses a first-party cookie to remember if you’ve accepted the policy – meaning after you accept, they won’t nag you repeatedly. - These sites also caution users that completely disabling cookies (via browser settings) can break site functionality. Instead, the preferred method is to use the provided banner or settings to selectively disable categories of cookies while keeping essential ones enabled.

categories.moreInfo: In summary, leading platforms combine clear **banner notices, easy opt-in/out options by category, and persistent preference centers** to comply with global requirements. Now, leveraging these best practices and findings, we will outline a comprehensive Cookie Policy for DoGood.

components.content: This Cookie Policy explains how and when DoGood (“we” or “us”) uses cookies and similar technologies on our website and applications (collectively, the “Platform”). It outlines what cookies are, the types of cookies we use, why we use them, and your choices regarding cookies. This Cookie Policy forms part of DoGood’s overall Privacy Policy. For more information on how we protect user data and privacy, please refer to our Privacy Policy. By using the DoGood Platform with cookies enabled in your browser settings, you consent to the use of cookies as described in this policy (to the extent required by law, we will obtain your explicit consent via the cookie banner on your first visit).

Cookies are small text files that websites send to your device (computer or mobile) to store information about you, such as your preferences or past actions. When you return to the site or navigate between pages, your browser sends these cookies back to the site’s server, allowing the website to “remember” your past activity. Cookies can be “session” cookies (temporary cookies that last only while your browser is open and are deleted when you close it) or “persistent” cookies (which remain on your device for a set period or until you delete them). Cookies set by DoGood (the website you are visiting) are called first-party cookies (used mainly for our own site functionality), whereas cookies set by other companies (integrated into our site for analytics, ads, etc.) are called third-party cookies. In addition to cookies, we may use similar tracking technologies like pixels, web beacons, or local storage – for simplicity, we refer to all of these as “cookies” in this policy

DoGood uses cookies and similar technologies to provide, protect, and improve our Platform’s services. For example, cookies help us to keep you logged in, remember your preferences, analyze how users use our site, and deliver content or ads that are relevant to you. Cookies play a key role in enabling us to fulfill our social impact mission effectively – they allow us to understand which features volunteers use the most, ensure secure and user-friendly interactions, and amplify our cause through targeted outreach.

To give you clarity, we’ve grouped the cookies on DoGood into four categories. You can choose to allow or disable non-essential categories through our cookie consent banner and Cookie Settings at any time (except Strictly Necessary cookies, which are always enabled for the reasons below).

items.description: These cookies are essential for the operation of our Platform and to use its core features. They enable basic functions like site navigation, login authentication, and form submissions, and they also help us ensure the **security and integrity** of our services. For instance, when you log into your DoGood account, we set a cookie to keep you logged in as you move between pages – without it, you would have to log in again on every page. We may also use necessary cookies to **protect our site** (e.g., a cookie that helps detect and prevent fraudulent activities or spam). For example, DoGood uses Google’s reCAPTCHA on our sign-up and contact forms to block bots – reCAPTCHA may set a cookie to determine if the user is human and not spam. Strictly Necessary cookies do not gather information about you for marketing or remember where you’ve been on the internet; they are only used to make our site function correctly. Because these cookies are vital for the website, they are deployed by default – **if you disable these cookies via your browser, some parts of the site will not work** (for example, you might not be able to log in, complete a donation, or see content relevant to your account).

Functional cookies allow DoGood to remember choices you make and provide enhanced, more personalized features. While not strictly necessary, they improve your user experience on our Platform. For example, these cookies might remember your preferred **language**, your location or region (to display relevant content), or other custom settings like whether you’ve dismissed a pop-up so we don’t show it again. Functional cookies also enable certain features: for instance, if we offer a live chat support or a user forum, a cookie may keep you logged in there or remember your alias. We also use these cookies to **facilitate your interactions with us** – a prime example is our integration of **HubSpot** (our customer support and communication tool). HubSpot sets cookies that store information you’ve entered in contact forms or our volunteer sign-up forms, so that if you return to our site on the same device, we recognize you and pre-fill your information. This saves you time and ensures continuity (and if you chat with us via our website chat widget, HubSpot’s cookie helps route you to the same agent you spoke with previously, improving service). Functional cookies can also help with **social media integration**: if you choose to share a DoGood campaign on Facebook or Twitter, a social plugin might use a cookie to remember that action or log you in to your social account. You can disable functional cookies if you prefer, but certain site features (like personalization or some forms of customer support) may not be available or may not remember your preferences.

Analytics cookies help us understand how visitors find and use our Platform, so we can learn what’s working and what’s not. They collect **aggregated, anonymous information** about site usage – for example, counting visits and traffic sources, seeing which pages are most popular, and observing how users move around the site. DoGood uses these insights to improve content and design, ensuring we create a better experience for our community. **Google Analytics** is one of the primary analytics tools we use. Google Analytics cookies (_ga, _gid, etc.) track things like how long you spend on our site, which pages you visit, and what actions you take. This information is aggregated — we look at trends among many users, not at individual behavior — and is not used to identify you personally. In fact, we have configured Google Analytics to anonymize IP addresses where applicable, and we do not combine Google Analytics data with any personal information you may provide to us. The analytics cookies tell us, for example, “100 people visited the volunteer opportunities page this week” or that one feature is used by 75% of logged-in users, etc. These insights guide us in making DoGood better. Besides Google Analytics, we may employ other analytics or performance measurement tools. For instance, we might use **Hotjar or Microsoft Clarity** for qualitative user experience analysis. These tools set cookies to track a single user session (so they know the same user scrolling on page A is the one clicking on page B). They can record anonymous information like where you click or how you scroll, which helps us spot UX problems or popular content. Rest assured, these session-recording tools **mask sensitive data** — any text you enter is hidden, and the recordings focus only on your site interactions (not personal details). Analytics cookies are **only placed if you opt** in via our cookie banner or settings. If you disable Analytics cookies, we will not collect this performance data about your visit, and it will be harder for us to know how our site is doing — but all core functions will still work for you.

Advertising or targeting cookies are used to **deliver content (such as ads or campaign messages) that are more relevant to you and to measure the effectiveness of our outreach efforts**. As a social impact platform, DoGood does not host third-party ads for profit, but we do run promotional campaigns to reach volunteers, donors, and partners (for example, we might advertise DoGood projects on platforms like Google, Facebook, or Instagram to attract more helpers). Advertising cookies on our site help us with these campaigns. For instance, we use the **Meta Pixel** (Facebook/Instagram) which sets cookies to track when a user comes to our site from a DoGood ad on Facebook and takes an action (like signing up for a volunteer project). This info helps us measure ad conversion and lets us retarget or reach people who showed interest. Similarly, we utilize **Google advertising cookies** (such as Google Ads and DoubleClick cookies) to monitor the performance of any Google Ads we run. These cookies remember that you visited DoGood and what actions you took, and if you later search Google or visit a site in the Google Ads network, they might enable DoGood promotional messages to be shown to you (“retargeting”). Advertising cookies may also be used to limit how often you see a particular ad and to help **customize messaging** so that it’s more relevant (for example, showing you a call-to-action for causes you’ve shown interest in, rather than something unrelated). The data from these cookies might include pseudonymous identifiers about your device and browser, and your browsing behavior on our site. **No personally identifying information (like your name or email) is contained in these cookies** but they do track device information that could be combined with other profiling data by our advertising partners. That’s why we ask for your consent before enabling Advertising cookies. If you opt in, you may see more tailored DoGood messages on other platforms; if you opt out, you’ll still see general DoGood ads or none at all, but the content might be less relevant to you. DoGood also honors the **“Do Not Sell My Personal Information”** principle under CCPA – which in this context means if you opt out of Advertising cookies, we will not share your cookie info with third-party advertising networks (effectively opting you out of any “sale” of data). Advertising cookies will not be set unless you give consent. You can always change your mind and disable them later via our Cookie Settings or by using industry opt-out tools (such as the NAI or YourAdChoices opt-out pages).

components.content: In implementing the above categories, DoGood works with a number of trusted third-party service providers who may set cookies on our behalf. Here is a non-exhaustive list of third-party tools we use (or may use) and what they do:

items.description: Analytics tool to collect usage data and generate site statistics. Cookies: _ga, _gid, etc. (persistent cookies lasting up to 2 years). These cookies help us count visitors and understand usage patterns. Data is sent to Google’s servers (which may be outside your country, e.g. the U.S.) in anonymized form. Opt-out: You can opt out of Google Analytics cookies via our Cookie Settings or by installing the [Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on](https://tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout) on your browser.

Advertising tool to measure the success of our Google ad campaigns and to retarget interested users. Cookies: e.g. _gcl_au (persistent, 90 days) and others from Google’s DoubleClick domain. These cookies track if you reached our site via a Google ad and help us optimize ad spend. They may also enable personalized DoGood ads on sites within Google’s network, if you have consented. [Opt-out: Disable “Advertising Cookies” in our preferences or adjust Google ad settings in your Google account.]

Advertising and social media retargeting tool for Facebook/Instagram. Cookies: e.g. fbp (Facebook Pixel ID cookie) and other Facebook domain cookies. Allows us to see when Facebook/Instagram users take actions on our site after viewing our ads. Helps in creating custom audiences and measuring ad conversions. [Opt-out: Disable “Advertising Cookies” or use Facebook’s ad preferences settings to control ads.]

User experience analytics tool that records anonymized user interactions (clicks, scrolls) and feedback. Cookies: _hjSession_*, _hjUser_*, etc. (short duration or persistent up to 1 year). These help Hotjar identify a user’s session across pages and whether it’s a first-time or returning visitor. Hotjar helps us improve site design by seeing aggregate behavior. [Opt-out: Disable “Analytics Cookies” in preferences. Hotjar also honors the Do Not Track header if enabled in your browser.]

An alternative to Hotjar we may use for session replay and heatmaps. Cookies: _clck, _clsk, CLID, etc. Clarity cookies gather information such as pages viewed, session duration, and interactions (including an anonymized session replay). Personal data is automatically masked. Used purely for our internal analysis and UX improvements. [Opt-out: Disable “Analytics Cookies”.]

CRM and marketing automation platform. Cookies: hubspotutk (tracks form submissions), hblid, __hstc and others. These cookies allow HubSpot to recognize returning visitors who have interacted with us (e.g. filled a form or chatted) and to track their site usage. They enable features like pre-filled forms and connecting you with the same support agent. HubSpot cookies are set only after you interact with certain parts of the site (like submitting a form) and if you consented to analytics/functional cookies. [Opt-out: If you disable “Functional/Analytics Cookies,” HubSpot tracking will be limited on our site. You can also clear your browser cookies to remove HubSpot identifiers.]

Customer Data Platform that helps route our analytics data. Cookies: ajs_anonymous_id, ajs_user_id (persistent up to 1 year). Segment cookies assign an anonymous ID to you so that all events (page views, clicks, sign-ups) can be correlated together and sent to our various analytics and marketing tools. This ensures consistency across analytics systems. Segment itself doesn’t use this data for any purpose other than to deliver it to our authorized destinations. [Opt-out: Disable “Analytics Cookies” to prevent Segment from tracking. Segment also supports respecting our Cookie Consent Management, so if you opt out, the Segment script will not run.]

items.type: Other Social Media and Content Widgets
items.description: If our site integrates with other platforms (for example, a **Twitter “Tweet” button**, a LinkedIn share widget, or embedded YouTube videos for showcasing projects), those services may set cookies. For instance, clicking “Share on Twitter” might allow Twitter to drop a cookie to remember that action or to see if you are logged into Twitter. An embedded YouTube video on a project page may set **YouTube’s** cookies which can track video views and user preferences. We endeavor to load such third-party content in a privacy-friendly mode (YouTube, for example, may be used in “privacy-enhanced mode” which limits tracking). Nonetheless, if you have **Advertising Cookies** disabled in our preferences, we will either block or ask for additional consent before loading any non-essential third-party content that sets cookies.

components.moreInfo: We will update the above list as our use of cookies and third-party tools changes over time. We aim to provide full transparency about any cookies and trackers in use.

components.type: Your Cookie Choices and How to Manage Cookies:
components.content: You have the right to choose whether or not to accept non-essential cookies. When you first visit DoGood, we will present a **cookie consent banner** that **allows you to accept all cookies**, or **refuse non-essential cookies**, or to customize your preference by category. We will not set Analytics, Functional, or Advertising cookies unless you opt in to those categories. Your selection will be remembered by a consent cookie so that on your next visit you won’t be prompted again (unless you clear your cookies or the law requires us to re-confirm consent periodically).
components.content2: If you change your mind later, **you can modify your cookie preferences at any time** by visiting our **[Cookie Settings]** (link available in the website footer and here). The Cookie Settings dashboard will show you the categories of cookies and your current consent status, and you can toggle your preferences (e.g., withdraw consent from Analytics cookies if you had previously allowed them, or vice versa). Any changes you make are applied immediately (for example, if you turn off Advertising cookies, we will stop using those cookies and the third parties will be instructed to not process or to delete any identifiable cookie data they have collected from our site).
components.content3: In addition to our cookie preference center, you can manage cookies through your **web browser settings**. Most browsers allow you to block or delete cookies (all cookies or by type or from specific websites). For example, you can typically find options under the “Privacy” or “Security” settings of your browser to clear browsing data (which deletes cookies) or to set rules for cookie acceptance. You can set your **browser to notify you when a cookie is being set** and choose to accept or refuse it. Please note, however, that if you disable all cookies through your browser (especially if you block even necessary cookies), our website may not function properly for you – you might not be able to log in, or some pages might not load correctly. For the best experience, we recommend using our built-in Cookie Settings to selectively control types of cookies, or using browser controls to **delete cookies** periodically if you wish, rather than a blanket block.
components.content4: If you are interested in broader opt-outs, here are some useful resources: - **Do Not Sell (CCPA Opt-Out)**: As mentioned, if you wish to opt out of the “sale”/sharing of your data for targeted advertising, simply disable Advertising cookies in our Cookie Settings. Alternatively, you can use the “Do Not Sell My Personal Information” link in our site footer (if you’re a California resident) which will achieve the same result by turning off all third-party marketing tags on our site. - **Industry opt-outs**: The Network Advertising Initiative (NAI) and Digital Advertising Alliance (DAA) offer web pages where you can globally opt out of interest-based advertising cookies from participating companies. [NAI Opt-out](https://thenai.org/how-to-opt-out/) | [DAA Opt-out](https://optout.aboutads.info/). Keep in mind this will not eliminate ads, but it can reduce targeted ads. - **Browser Do Not Track**: Our site honors “Do Not Track” signals for analytics and advertising cookies. If your browser is set to Send a Do Not Track request, our cookies (aside from strictly necessary) will default to disabled. (However, not all browsers or third parties consistently support DNT, so using our explicit opt-outs as described above is more reliable.)
